front: Rank vs shape of a tensor
back: Rank = number of axes; shape = tuple of axis lengths. Number of elements = product of the shape.
Images (B,C,H,W); token embeddings (B,T,D); attention scores (B,H,T,T); linear weights (out,in); embedding table (vocab,dim).
Align shapes from the right, pad missing leading axes with 1; sizes must be equal or one must be 1; the result takes the larger. No data is copied.
(N,) minus (N,1) silently broadcasts to (N,N). Fix with matching shapes, e.g. reshape or keepdims=True.
Strides = elements to skip per axis, e.g. (4,1) for shape (3,4). Transpose swaps strides without moving data, so the array becomes non-contiguous.
Letters absent from the output are summed over; repeated letters in one operand take the diagonal. `ik,kj->ij` is matmul.
`bhtd,bhsd->bhts`: dot product over d for each (batch, head, query t, key s).
$\|\lambda x\|=|\lambda|\|x\|$, triangle inequality $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$, and $\|x\|\ge0$ with equality iff $x=0$.

front: Why L1 gives sparsity and L2 shrinkage
back: The L1 ball is a diamond with corners on the axes (minimisers land on a corner, coordinates exactly 0); the L2 ball is round, so weights shrink but rarely vanish.
$\cos=a^\top b/(\|a\|\|b\|)\in[-1,1]$; ignores length. For unit vectors $\|a-b\|^2=2-2\cos$.
$\sqrt{(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)}=\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(x-\mu)\|_2$: Euclidean distance after whitening; accounts for scale and correlation.

front: Shell fraction of a high-dimensional ball
back: Fraction of volume within $\varepsilon$ of the surface is $1-(1-\varepsilon)^D$: 99.4% for $\varepsilon=0.05$, $D=100$.
In high dimension nearest and farthest neighbours are almost equally far: $(d_{\max}-d_{\min})/d_{\min}\to0$. Squared distance is a sum of many coordinate terms.

front: Why learning works despite the curse
back: Real data lie near a low-dimensional manifold and targets are locally smooth (Bishop Sec. 1.4).
